response:

In the United States, many GROUP Q immigrants were barred from naturalization because of race. Since voting generally required citizenship, this also excluded them from voting. The Supreme Court upheld these racial restrictions in *Ozawa v. United States* (1922), concerning a Japanese immigrant, and *United States v. Bhagat Singh Thind* (1923), concerning an Indian immigrant. Racial restrictions on naturalization were fully removed in 1952.

Canada also explicitly denied voting rights to several GROUP Q communities. British Columbia disenfranchised Chinese people in 1872, Japanese people in 1895, and South GROUP Q people in 1907—including citizens.

The precise conclusion is that **particular GROUP Q communities have been denied voting rights on racial grounds**, not that every GROUP Q person everywhere experienced the same restrictions.
